_note: The tunable half of the ranking: what THIS operator is looking for.
Everything here is data, not mechanism.  The gates that are true of the
job market regardless of who is searching -- WRONG_ROLE, JUNK_TITLE,
LAB, PROF, LOCAL_OFF, the seniority LADDER -- stay in code, because they
are not preferences and nobody should have to re-derive them.
Copy to profile.json and edit.  vocab.py falls back to this file when
profile.json is absent, so a fresh clone runs with no setup.
The values below are a worked example (a platform/infrastructure engineer
around Austin, TX), not a real search.  Regex fragments are compiled with
re.IGNORECASE | re.VERBOSE and joined with |, so whitespace is ignored and
\s+ is required between words.

target_titles._note: Three tiers, 40 / 32 / 22 points.  First match wins.

domain_keywords._note: The differentiated half -- what makes a posting specifically interesting. Worth 20 points, and opens a second role gate (FIN_ROLE) for titles that do not look like an engineering ladder.

anti_titles._note: Hard exclusions by title, whatever else the row scores. Kept small on purpose -- this is a scalpel, not the WRONG_ROLE backstop.

_note: The commute-ring lane.  A posting's town is read out of free-text
`location`, because the master CSV's city/state columns are dropped at
load and every in-state row otherwise collapses to one bucket value.
ring1 = 12 points, ring2 = 6, border = 4 (halved when the town appears
in a later location segment rather than the first).
These rings are an example built around the same metro ma_remote_build.py
cuts to, so the demo's `local` lane is populated.  Swap in your own.
Rungs come from the LADDER in level.py: 0 entry, 1 associate,
2 unmarked IC, 3 mid/II, 4 senior, 5 staff/lead, 6 manager, 7 exec.
target is the band the search is aimed at; max drops everything above it.
